Paging

The page unit translates every user-mode main-memory cycle through a page table before the DRAM controller sees it. It gives each program a private 4 MiB address space built from 4 KiB pages, and it refuses any access the table does not grant. Return to the main page.

Supervisor cycles bypass translation entirely and see flat physical memory, so the BIOS reaches all 4 MiB and can load tables while a program is stopped. Supervisor Protection covers the I/O region and the firmware ROM; this document covers main memory.

1. Purpose and Limits

Supervisor protection stops an application from reaching hardware. It does nothing to stop one application from overwriting another, because both run in the same flat DRAM. The page unit closes that gap: a user-mode cycle reaches physical memory only through a table entry the BIOS wrote, so two programs share the machine without sharing each other's memory.

Programs also stop caring where they sit in physical memory. Every context sees the same logical layout, so the BIOS loads a program at whatever frames are free and fixes the addresses in the table rather than in the code.

No Demand Paging

The MC68EC000 pushes a bus-error stack frame that does not support instruction continuation. A faulting instruction cannot be resumed, so the BIOS cannot fetch a missing page and retry. Demand paging and swapping need a processor that can restart a bus cycle, and this one cannot.

Every page a program touches is therefore resident for as long as the program runs. What the unit provides is relocation, isolation between programs, and per-page write protection. A fault is a fatal error, not a request for service.

2. Translation Model

A user-mode cycle in $000000-$3FFFFF splits into a page number and an offset. The table replaces the page number; the offset passes through untouched. 

logical  A23..A22  A21..A12   A11..A0
                   page       offset
                     |           |
                  page table     |
                     |           |
physical           PPN       A11..A0
                 A21..A12

Ten bits of page number cover the whole 4 MiB logical space, and ten bits of physical frame number cover the whole 4 MiB of DRAM. Logical and physical spaces are the same size, so a context can in principle map every frame, and in practice the BIOS keeps most entries invalid.

Which cycles are translated
Cycle Address range Behavior
User mode, main memory $000000-$3FFFFF Translated; an invalid entry faults.
Supervisor, main memory $000000-$3FFFFF Untranslated; logical address is the physical address.
Either, anywhere else Outside $000000-$3FFFFF Untouched by this unit. The expansion windows, the VGA aperture, and the I/O region keep their revision 1.1 decode, subject to supervisor protection.

Translation stays clear of the DRAM row address by construction. The DRAM address multiplexer builds its row from CPU A1..A10 and its column from A11..A20, and the bank select comes from A21. A 4 KiB page leaves A11..A0 untranslated, so the entire translated field lands in the column address and the bank select. The row address is ready as soon as the processor drives it, whatever the table says.

3. Page Table Entry

An entry is one 16-bit word. Two chips give the table its width: the upper holds bits 15 through 8 and the lower holds bits 7 through 0.

Page table entry format
Bits Name Meaning
15 V Valid. When clear, any user-mode access to the page faults.
14 W Writable. When clear, a user-mode read succeeds and a user-mode write faults.
13 through 10 Reserved Write zero. The hardware ignores them and a later revision may define them.
9 through 0 PPN Physical frame number, driven onto physical A21..A12.

An invalid entry still drives a frame number onto the physical address bus, because the SRAM has no way to withhold it. That costs nothing: the page unit withholds both bank requests instead, so the DRAM controller never starts a cycle and the frame number goes nowhere.

A read-only page shares the same path. The unit compares W against R/W and withholds the requests on a write, so the DRAM sees no cycle at all rather than a cycle it must abandon.

4. Table Storage and Indexing

U_PAGE_TBL_H and U_PAGE_TBL_L are CY7C199-20VC 32K x 8 static RAMs sharing one address bus. Together they hold 32768 entries of 16 bits, which is 32 contexts of 1024 pages, and the design uses all of it.

Index Wiring

The low ten address lines of both chips connect straight to the processor. Nothing sits between them. 

SRAM A9..A0   <-- CPU A21..A12
SRAM A14..A10 <-- context register, U_PAGE_MMU

This is the piece that keeps the unit small. During a translated cycle CPU A21..A12 is the logical page number. During a table access CPU A21..A12 is the entry number, because the aperture is placed where those lines are free to carry it. One wiring serves both, so the unit needs no address multiplexer, no buffers on the index, and no CPLD pins to carry it. The lookup also starts the instant the processor drives the address, with nothing ahead of it.

/CE on both chips connects to ground, so the lookup runs on every address the processor drives and the entry is waiting at the output stage before anything asks for it. TBL_OE_n in section 7 decides whether that entry reaches the bus. Gating /CE would save current at the cost of tACE on every lookup, and the lookup is the one thing this design keeps short.

Context Register

The five upper address lines come from a register in U_PAGE_MMU. Switching contexts is a single write, so a context switch costs the BIOS one bus cycle rather than a table reload.

Reset clears the register to context 0. Supervisor cycles do not consult the table, so the BIOS may change the register at any moment without disturbing its own memory access.

5. Table Aperture

Memory map revision 1.2 left $A00000-$DFFFFF unimplemented, and EXP_MEM5_n and EXP_MEM6_n were decoded but reached nothing. Revision 2.0 gives those 4 MiB to the page table, which is the only place on the board where CPU A21..A12 is free to carry an entry number.

Entry Addresses

The two regions are each 2 MiB and the pair is not 4 MiB aligned, so A21 reads back as 1 in region 5 and 0 in region 6. Entry numbers therefore split across the two regions, with the lower half in the upper region.

Where each entry appears
Entry Address Region
0 through 511 $C00000 + N * 4096 6, A21 = 0
512 through 1023 $A00000 + (N - 512) * 4096 5, A21 = 1

Entries are 4096 bytes apart because the index rides on A21..A12 and A11..A1 are not decoded. Each entry therefore repeats through its own 4 KiB block. Firmware walks the table by adding 4096 to a pointer, and crosses from one base to the other at entry 512.

Access Rules

  • Word accesses read and write a whole entry. Byte accesses reach one chip each: UDS_n gates the upper chip and LDS_n the lower. The upper byte carries V, W, and the top two bits of the frame number, so changing a permission bit means reading that byte, altering it, and writing it back. The lower byte holds PPN7..PPN0 and nothing else.
  • The aperture addresses the current context only. To build another context's table, select that context, write the entries, and select the original again.
  • A user-mode access to the aperture faults. U_PAGE_MMU checks FC2 itself, so the supervisor-protection decoder needs no term for these two regions.
  • The page unit acknowledges its own cycles with PAGE_DTACK_n and adds no wait states. The CY7C199-20 answers in 20 ns against a bus cycle of 400 ns.

6. Control Registers

I/O slot 10, $F40000-$F5FFFF, carries the two controls. Both encode their value in the address and ignore the data, in the same style as SYSREG0. Both are write-only and both sit inside the protected I/O region, so only the BIOS reaches them.

Page-unit control registers
Address Name Effect
$F40001 + 2C, C = 0 to 31 PAGECTX Selects context C. The value rides on A5..A1.
$F40041 PAGEOFF Disables translation. Every cycle passes through untranslated, as it did in revision 1.1.
$F40043 PAGEON Enables translation for user-mode main-memory cycles.

A6 separates the two groups: low selects a context, high selects the enable control. A16..A7 are not decoded, so both groups repeat through the slot; firmware uses the canonical addresses above.

Reset clears the context register to 0 and clears the enable bit, so the machine comes up with translation off. That is the right state for reset, because the BIOS has no table yet, and it is the right state for bringing the board up, because it makes the page unit transparent without removing it.

With the bit clear there is no main-memory protection at all: a user-mode program reaches every frame, including the vectors in frame 0. Translation must be on before the first RTE into user mode, and it should stay on.

7. Physical Address Bus

PPA9..PPA0 carries physical A21..A12 to the DRAM address multiplexer and to the bank logic. Exactly one driver holds it at any time.

Who drives the physical page bus
Condition PPA9..PPA8 PPA7..PPA0
Translated cycle U_PAGE_TBL_H and U_PAGE_TBL_L data outputs, PTE bits 9 through 0
Aperture read The same two data outputs, carrying the entry the processor asked for
Aperture write U_PAGE_XCVR_H and U_PAGE_XCVR_L, passing CPU D9..D0 to the table
Any other cycle U_PAGE_MMU, copying CPU A21..A20 U_PHYS_BUF, copying CPU A19..A12

U_PHYS_BUF is an SN74HCT244N. FAST is not needed here: the column address is not selected until 50 ns after RAS falls, which is hundreds of nanoseconds after the processor drove the address, and an HCT buffer presents a 1 uA load to the address bus instead of the 0.6 mA a FAST buffer would.

U_PAGE_MMU drives the top two bits itself rather than through a second buffer, because it already needs A21 for the untranslated bank select. Its PPA9 output shares one I/O pin with the PPN9 input it reads back from the table: the macrocell drives the pin while the table is quiet and reads the same net while the table holds it.

Bus Enables

U_PAGE_MMU produces the bus enables, and two terms settle them. TBL_DRIVE marks a user-mode cycle with translation turned on, whatever address the processor is driving. APERTURE marks a cycle that has reached the table through the two decoded regions. 

TBL_DRIVE  = (NOT FC2) AND PAGE_ENABLE
APERTURE   = (NOT EXP_MEM5_n) OR (NOT EXP_MEM6_n)
TBL_OE_n   = NOT (TBL_DRIVE OR (APERTURE AND R/W))
PHYS_OE_n  = TBL_DRIVE OR APERTURE

PHYS_OE_n gates the PPA9 and PPA8 drivers as well as U_PHYS_BUF, so the buffer and the two MACH outputs turn on and off together. That leaves one source on PPA9..PPA0 at any moment: the table while TBL_DRIVE holds or an aperture read is under way, the transceivers through an aperture write, and U_PHYS_BUF with U_PAGE_MMU the rest of the time. The bus is driven in all four cases and never floats.

TBL_DRIVE rests on FC2 and a stored bit and on nothing the decoder produces, so it settles before the processor asserts AS_n and no lookup ever waits on an enable. The enables change between bus cycles, when FC2 changes, and a few nanoseconds of skew between them can let the SRAM and the buffer drive together briefly. Both parts tolerate that; confirm on the assembled board that the overlap stays short enough not to disturb the supply.

V and W reach U_PAGE_MMU on upper-chip pins that only the table and its transceiver ever hold, so they float on any cycle that turns both off. Fit a 10 kohm pull-down on each rather than leave a CMOS input to drift. PERMIT ignores both bits on an untranslated cycle, so the pull-downs guard the input stage rather than the logic.

DRAM Connection

PPA8..PPA0 --> column inputs of the DRAM address mux, DRAM A9..A1
CPU A11    --> column input of the DRAM address mux, DRAM A0
CPU A10..A1 --> row inputs, DRAM A9..A0, unchanged
PPA9       --> bank select inside U_PAGE_MMU

The multiplexer itself does not change. Nine of its ten column inputs simply take the page unit's output where they used to take CPU A20..A12. The DRAM document keeps ownership of the multiplexer and the strobe timing.

8. Bank Requests

The address decoder produces logical requests. The page unit consumes them, decides which physical bank the cycle belongs to, and produces the requests the DRAM controller acts on. 

LRAM_REQ    = (NOT LRAM0_REQ_n) OR (NOT LRAM1_REQ_n)
TRANSLATE   = LRAM_REQ AND (NOT FC2) AND PAGE_ENABLE
WRITE       = NOT R/W
PERMIT      = (NOT TRANSLATE) OR (V AND (W OR (NOT WRITE)))
PHYS_BANK1  = TRANSLATE ? PPN9 : A21

RAM0_REQ_n  = NOT (LRAM_REQ AND PERMIT AND (NOT PHYS_BANK1))
RAM1_REQ_n  = NOT (LRAM_REQ AND PERMIT AND PHYS_BANK1)

A supervisor cycle sets TRANSLATE low, so PERMIT is true and the bank follows CPU A21. The result is the revision 1.1 behavior exactly: LRAM0_REQ_n becomes RAM0_REQ_n and LRAM1_REQ_n becomes RAM1_REQ_n, one gate delay later.

A translated cycle ignores which logical bank the decoder picked and uses the frame number instead. A logical page in bank 0 can map to a frame in bank 1 and the other way round, which is what makes the physical pool a single pool.

The boot overlay still suppresses bank 0 through ALIAS_ACTIVE, inside LRAM0_REQ_n, before the page unit sees it. Nothing in the overlay path changes.

9. Page Faults

Three conditions fault, and all three produce the same result: no bank request, no DRAM cycle, and /BERR to the processor.

Fault conditions
Condition Test
Invalid page Translated cycle with V = 0
Write to a read-only page Translated write with V = 1 and W = 0
User-mode access to the table aperture EXP_MEM5_n or EXP_MEM6_n active with FC2 low 
PAGE_FAULT  = (TRANSLATE AND NOT PERMIT)
              OR (APERTURE AND NOT FC2)
PAGE_BERR_n = NOT PAGE_FAULT

PAGE_BERR_n joins the timeout, the interrupt abort, and the protection violation inside U_PROT, which drives the processor's /BERR pin. It releases when the logical request releases, which happens when the processor negates AS_n.

Fault Timing

A fault waits on the logical request, which is the slowest input involved. Worst case that is AS_n through the normal-cycle gate, the qualifier buffer, and the two bank-request gates, then U_PAGE_MMU and U_PROT. 

AS_n
  -> NORMAL_CYCLE_n      30 ns
  -> NORMAL_MEM_n        42 ns
  -> LRAM0_BASE_n        30 ns
  -> LRAM0_REQ_n         30 ns
  -> PAGE_BERR_n         12 ns
  -> BERR_n              15 ns

worst case               159 ns after AS_n

The DRAM controller needs longer than that to answer a successful cycle: it waits for a byte strobe, passes two 20 MHz synchronizer stages, and then runs a RAS and CAS sequence. A faulting cycle therefore ends sooner than a successful one, and the fault costs the processor nothing beyond the exception itself.

TBL_OE_n falls out of FC2 and the enable bit rather than out of the decoder, so the table outputs are already live when the processor drives the address. V and W are valid 20 ns later and are never the late input.

What the Handler Sees

The bus-error handler cannot resume the instruction, so it terminates the program. It separates a page fault from the other bus-error sources by looking at the stacked fault address and status register: a fault inside $000000-$3FFFFF with the supervisor bit clear came from this unit. Hardware provides no status register for faults, because the three conditions are distinguishable in software from the table the BIOS wrote.

10. Worked Examples

User-Mode Read at $013500, Page Mapped

Logical page 19 is mapped to frame 300 with V = 1 and W = 1. The offset within the page is $500. 

FC2              = 0       user
A21..A12         = 0000010011 = 19
SRAM A9..A0      = 19
context          = 3
SRAM A14..A10    = 3

PTE              = $C12C    V=1 W=1 PPN=300
PPA9..PPA0       = 300 = 0100101100
PHYS_BANK1       = PPA9 = 0

PERMIT           = 1
RAM0_REQ_n       = 0
RAM1_REQ_n       = 1

physical address = 300 * 4096 + $500 = $12C500

The DRAM controller starts a bank 0 cycle. Its row address came from CPU A10..A1 and never waited on the table.

User-Mode Write to a Read-Only Page

The same program writes to logical page 19 after the BIOS cleared W to share the page with another context. 

FC2              = 0
R/W              = 0       write
PTE              = $812C   V=1 W=0 PPN=300

PERMIT           = V AND (W OR NOT WRITE)
                 = 1 AND (0 OR 0)
                 = 0

RAM0_REQ_n       = 1
RAM1_REQ_n       = 1
PAGE_BERR_n      = 0

No DRAM cycle begins, so the page keeps its contents. The processor takes a bus error and the BIOS ends the program.

Supervisor Read at $013500

FC2              = 1       supervisor
TRANSLATE        = 0
PERMIT           = 1

PPA9..PPA0       = CPU A21..A12 = 19
PHYS_BANK1       = A21 = 0
RAM0_REQ_n       = 0

physical address = $013500

The BIOS sees flat memory. Logical page 19 is frame 19 for supervisor code regardless of what context 3 says.

Writing Entry 700

Entry 700 is in the upper half, so it appears in region 5 at $A00000 + (700 - 512) * 4096, which is $ABC000. 

CPU address      = $ABC000
A21              = 1       upper half
A20..A12         = 188
SRAM A9..A0      = 700

FC2              = 1       supervisor, so no fault
EXP_MEM5_n       = 0
U_PAGE_XCVR_H/_L enabled, XCVR_DIR low, CPU D15..D0 to the table
SRAM /WE pulsed on both chips for a word write
PAGE_DTACK_n     = 0

11. Package and Pin Assignments

Page-unit packages
Reference Part Function
U_PAGE_MMU MACH210-12JC, 44-pin PLCC Context register, enable bit, control decode, permission test, bank requests, fault, and all enables
U_PAGE_TBL_H CY7C199-20VC Page table entry bits 15 through 8
U_PAGE_TBL_L CY7C199-20VC Page table entry bits 7 through 0
U_PAGE_XCVR_H SN74HCT245N CPU D15..D8 to the upper table chip
U_PAGE_XCVR_L SN74HCT245N CPU D7..D0 to the lower table chip
U_PHYS_BUF SN74HCT244N CPU A19..A12 onto PPA7..PPA0 when not translating

U_PAGE_MMU Signals

The MACH210 offers 38 signal pins in the 44-pin PLCC, of which at most 32 can be outputs. The lists below name 21 inputs and 17 outputs, but PPN9 and PPA9 share one I/O pin, so the design occupies 37 pins and leaves one spare. Fifteen macrocells are unused as well, though the one free pin is what limits any later addition.

U_PAGE_MMU inputs
Signal Count Purpose
FC2 1 Privilege level of the current cycle.
R/W 1 Direction, for the W test.
RESET_n 1 Clears the context register and the enable bit.
LRAM0_REQ_n, LRAM1_REQ_n 2 Logical bank requests from the address decoder.
EXP_MEM5_n, EXP_MEM6_n 2 Table aperture select.
IO10_n 1 Control register slot select.
CPU A21, A20 2 Untranslated bank select and the top two bits of the pass-through physical address.
CPU A6..A1 6 Control register select and value.
UDS_n, LDS_n 2 Byte lanes for table writes.
PTE V, W, PPN9 3 Permission bits and the translated bank bit, read back from the table. PPN9 shares the PPA9 pin and reads it back while that output is tri-stated.
U_PAGE_MMU outputs
Signal Count Purpose
SRAM A14..A10 5 Context register.
TBL_OE_n, to SRAM /OE 1 Low while TBL_DRIVE holds or an aperture read is under way; high through an aperture write and on every untranslated cycle, so the table never fights U_PHYS_BUF.
SRAM /WE_H, /WE_L 2 Byte-selected table writes.
XCVR_OE_n 1 Enables both transceivers for an aperture cycle.
XCVR_DIR 1 Direction for both transceivers, a buffered copy of R/W. Driving it from the MACH keeps two loads off the processor's R/W net, which runs close to its limit at revision 2.0.
PHYS_OE_n 1 Enables U_PHYS_BUF when neither the table nor the transceivers hold PPA9..PPA0.
PPA9, PPA8 2 Pass-through physical address bits, enabled and tri-stated by PHYS_OE_n alongside U_PHYS_BUF.
RAM0_REQ_n, RAM1_REQ_n 2 Physical bank requests to the DRAM controller.
PAGE_DTACK_n 1 Completion for aperture and control cycles, into U_DTACK_B gate 1 pin 5.
PAGE_BERR_n 1 Page fault, into U_PROT.

The context register and the enable bit are the only storage in the device. Everything else is combinatorial. Pin assignment waits on the fitting report, because the MACH switch matrix constrains which block a signal can reach; record the report alongside the schematic.

Every package here is socketed and carries a 100 nF capacitor and a 1 uF capacitor in parallel across its supply pins, beside the socket, as elsewhere on the board. The MACH210 and the two SRAMs switch harder than the 74-series parts around them, so give each its own pair rather than sharing.

12. Timing Verification

Datasheet values used here
Device Path Symbol Maximum Source
CY7C199-20 Address to data valid tAA 20 ns CY7C199, switching characteristics
CY7C199-20 /OE low to data valid tDOE 9 ns CY7C199, switching characteristics
CY7C199-20 /OE high to high impedance tHZOE 9 ns CY7C199, switching characteristics
CY7C199-20 Write cycle time and write pulse width tWC / tPWE 20 ns / 15 ns CY7C199, write cycle
MACH210-12 Input or feedback to combinatorial output tPD 12 ns MACH210, MACH210-12 commercial
SN74HCT244 A to Y tpd 42 ns SN74HCT244, section 5.5
SN74HCT245 A to B or B to A tpd 42 ns SN74HCT245, switching characteristics

Translation Path

Delays from a valid CPU address
Result Stages Total Needed by
PTE valid on PPA9..PPA0 CY7C199 tAA 20 ns Column select, 50 ns after RAS falls
PPA9..PPA0 on an untranslated cycle SN74HCT244 tpd 42 ns Same
Permission decision inside the MACH 20 ns + 12 ns 32 ns Request capture
RAM0_REQ_n from the address path 45 ns + 30 ns + 30 ns + 12 ns 117 ns Request capture
RAM0_REQ_n from the strobe path AS_n + 30 ns + 42 ns + 30 ns + 30 ns + 12 ns 144 ns after AS_n Request capture
RAM1_REQ_n from the strobe path AS_n + 30 ns + 42 ns + 30 ns + 12 ns 114 ns after AS_n Request capture

The page unit adds one 12 ns stage to the bank requests and nothing at all to the row address. The DRAM controller waits for a byte strobe and two 20 MHz synchronizer stages before it asserts RAS, so 12 ns does not move the start of a DRAM cycle. The column address has even more room: it is not selected until 50 ns after RAS falls, and the table answers in 20 ns from the processor's own address.

Aperture Cycle

A table read presents the SRAM output to the processor through a transceiver: 20 ns for the lookup and 42 ns for the transceiver, well inside a 400 ns bus cycle acknowledged with no wait states. A table write needs the 15 ns write pulse; the processor holds address and data for the remainder of the cycle after U_PAGE_MMU releases /WE, so every setup and hold in the write table is met by a wide margin.

U_PAGE_MMU ends the write pulse when the qualified aperture select releases, which the processor does by negating its data strobes while it still drives the bus. That order matters: a write must never end after the data has gone.

Bench Checks

  • With translation off, confirm the machine behaves exactly as revision 1.1: same DRAM timing, same acknowledge, no faults.
  • Confirm the physical page bus is driven at all times and that the overlap between U_PHYS_BUF and the table outputs is short.
  • Measure RAM0_REQ_n and RAM1_REQ_n against the DRAM controller's request capture and confirm the extra stage has not moved RAS.
  • Fault a known page and confirm /BERR arrives before the controller would have acknowledged.

Noise margins across the page unit
Driver Receiver High margin Low margin Status
MC68EC000 address output CY7C199 address input 1.80 V 0.30 V Compatible

The tightest figure is the 0.20 V between a MACH210 output and a CY7C199 address input, because the SRAM asks for 2.2 V where most TTL parts ask for 2.0 V. The MACH210 guarantees 2.4 V while sourcing 3.2 mA, and the five context lines each drive two SRAM inputs drawing 5 uA apiece, so the real output sits close to the rail rather than at the guaranteed floor. Measure one context line on the assembled board and record the figure.

Load Added to the Processor Buses

New loads on existing nets
Net Added loads Added current Added capacitance
CPU A21, A20 2 SRAM inputs and 1 MACH input 20 uA About 22 pF
CPU A19..A12 2 SRAM inputs and 1 HCT244 input 11 uA About 22 pF
CPU A6..A1 1 MACH input 10 uA 6 pF
FC2, UDS_n, LDS_n, RESET_n 1 MACH input each 10 uA 6 pF
CPU R/W 1 MACH input 10 uA 6 pF
CPU D15..D0 1 HCT245 input each 1 uA 10 pF
IO10_n, EXP_MEM5_n, EXP_MEM6_n 1 MACH input each 10 uA 6 pF

Everything the page unit adds is CMOS, so the static current is negligible against the processor's 400 uA source and 3.2 mA sink. The capacitance matters more: A19..A12 pick up roughly 22 pF each, on top of whatever the decoder and the DRAM multiplexer already present. The motherboard load audit keeps CPU nets at or below 100 pF against the processor's 130 pF limit, and these figures belong in it. The SRAM datasheet gives no input capacitance, so 8 pF per input is assumed here and has to be confirmed.

R/W is the net to watch. It already carried ten loads at revision 1.1, the VGA grant qualifier in U_OR6 gate 4 adds an eleventh, and U_PAGE_MMU a twelfth, which puts it near 116 pF before any trace. Both transceiver direction pins take XCVR_DIR from the MACH for that reason; wiring them to R/W instead would add 20 pF and leave nothing for the board. The revision 2.0 load audit carries the figure as an open item.

14. Power

+5 V current added by the page unit
Part Current Basis
U_PAGE_MMU 120 mA typical MACH210-12 ICC at 25 MHz with a 16-bit counter pattern; this design switches far less
U_PAGE_TBL_H and _L up to 150 mA each CY7C199-20 maximum operating current, specified at the maximum cycle rate. The table is addressed at bus speed, not at 50 MHz, so the real figure is well below this
Two HCT245 and one HCT244 Under 1 mA static each HCT quiescent current; dynamic current follows switching

Revision 1.1 carried no protection logic, so nothing comes off the rail against this, and U_PROT adds 55 mA of its own. An earlier draft of this section took an 85 mA credit for the five FAST packages that the first revision 2.0 protection draft would have used; those packages never reached a board, so the credit was not real. The honest planning figure for the whole revision 2.0 change is about 480 mA of headline maximum and appreciably less in practice, because both SRAM figures assume a 50 MHz cycle rate this bus never reaches. Take it to the power control budget before layout rather than after.

Gating the SRAM /CE would cut the table current by about four fifths, at the cost of tACE on every lookup. That trade is available later if the rail turns out tight, and the timing margin above can absorb it.

15. Firmware Rules

The hardware enforces the table. The BIOS decides what the table says, and a few of its decisions are what keep the rest of the machine safe.

  1. Never map a firmware frame into a user context. Frames 0 through 31 hold the exception vectors and BIOS private memory at $000000-$01FFFF. The hardware has no term that stops the BIOS from mapping them, and a program that reached frame 0 could rewrite a TRAP vector and take supervisor mode. This is the single rule the privilege model rests on.
  2. Invalidate before reuse. A context's table holds whatever the last program left in it, and the SRAM powers up with random contents. Clear all 1024 entries of a context before giving it to a program.
  3. Turn translation on before the first user-mode instruction, and leave it on. With the enable bit clear the page unit passes everything through and main memory has no protection. Supervisor cycles never consult the table, so the bit costs the BIOS nothing and there is no reason to clear it again.
  4. Do not share a writable page between contexts unless both programs are meant to see each other's writes. Shared read-only pages are safe and are what the W bit is for.
  5. Close the VGA grant when the program stops. The grant in SYSREG2 is not part of the page table and does not follow a context switch.
  6. Check BIOS call arguments against the caller's table, not against a fixed range. A pointer that a program passes to the BIOS is a logical address in its own context, and the BIOS runs untranslated. Translate it in software before touching it, and reject it if the entry is invalid or the call would write a page with W clear.

Rule 6 replaces the fixed range check that the call gate described before paging existed. The two documents agree: the gate validates, the page unit does not validate on the BIOS's behalf.

Boot Order

  1. Reset. Translation is off and the context register is 0.
  2. The BIOS initialises DRAM and disables the boot overlay, exactly as before.
  3. The BIOS writes its exception vectors into physical $000000-$0003FF, which it reaches untranslated.
  4. The BIOS clears context 0's table, maps the program it wants to run, and writes $F40043 to enable translation.
  5. The BIOS selects the program's context and enters it with RTE.
